I’d like to offer some spiritual advice so that you can read Scripture the way that Jesus did and use it for good purposes. Offer a prayer for guidance from the Holy Spirit before you make your interpretation of an important text. With an open heart and mind, seek the attitude of a beginner and learner. Pray as long as it takes to feel any certitudes loosen. Once you have attained some degree of openness, try to move to a position of detachment from your own egoic will and its goals and desires—to be correct, to be secure, to stay with the familiar. This might take some time, but without such freedom from your own need for control, you will invariably make a text say what you need and want it to say. Then you must listen for a deeper voice than your own, which you will know because it will never shame or frighten you, but rather strengthen you, even when it is challenging you. If it is God’s voice, it will take away your illusions and your violence so completely and so naturally that you can barely identify with such previous feelings! I call this God’s replacement therapy. God does not ask and expect you to do anything new until God has first made it desirable and possible for you to do it. Grace cannot easily operate under coercion, duress, shame, or guilt. If your understanding of Scripture leads you to experience any or several of the fruits of the Spirit—love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, trustfulness, gentleness, and self-control (Galatians 5:22-23)—I think you can trust that this interpretation is from the Spirit, from the deeper stream of wisdom. As you read, if you sense any negative or punitive emotions like morose delight, feelings of superiority, self-satisfaction, arrogant dualistic certitude, desire for revenge, need for victory, or a spirit of dismissal or exclusion, you must trust that this is not Jesus’ hermeneutic at work, but your own ego still steering the ship. Remember the temptation of Jesus in the desert (Matthew 4:3-10). Three temptations to the misuse of power are listed: economic, religious, and political. Even Jesus must face these subtle disguises before he begins his public ministry. Only when he has found freedom from his own egoic need for power can Jesus teach with true inner authority and speak truth to the oppressive powers of his time.

// so let's take these information processing thoughts to a considation of facts, or rather the meaning of "facts". These are thought to be objective, perhaps the outcomes of observation, through some clever philosophers of science talk about theory-laden facts, as if our theories are built into our observations. So, for example, particles like the Higgs Boson are observed, indirecly, via statistical analysis of a great many collisions at the LHC, recorded in one of its general purpose detectors, CMS or ATLAS; that statistical analysis builds on recontruction of many individual events, each of which is reconstructed from some behavior in the detector, and some basic information about the energy of the colliding particles. The reconstruction of the daughter particles emerging from the collision of parents is tough, because in advance you can't know what the nature of the parent particles are: protons are not fundamental, and the number and nature of the constituent particles--quarks and gluons--from each proton are numerous, and can only be identified through reconstructions, solutions that are consistent with the laws of nature and all of the more basic observations in the detector (such as the number of electrons flowing out of a photomultiplier tube (that is, the current) of a known voltage and a feed of photons from a scintillator of known properties, between layers n and n+1 of brass of known thickness and properties. In the end, we know what daughter particles, and in what directions they traveled with what speed, emerged from each initial collision. To find the Higgs, we need to interpret that data for each collision as whole, and find patterns that emerge in the production of many such events that are consistent with the known laws of nature probably (at a 99.99999% confidence level) only if the Higgs Boson exists under such laws. But to do even a single reconstruction of a single collision, we need to know what all the emergent (daughter) particles are; we need to detect them, and that's what the detector (CMS or ATLAS) is for. But it turns out that there is a type of particle--neutrinos--which we can detect, but only rarely and with much more detector than we could afford to build around the LHC. But we can apply some pretty basic physical theory (convervation of momentum) to the problem, infer the existence and kind of neutrinos which must have been produced, and use these to complete the picture of all the collision products, reason back to the nature of the colliding parent particles, and use the many emerging complete accounts of individual collisions to find patterns (perhaps predicted by theory, perhaps not) that emerge through many such events. In such a way, human kind discovered the Higgs Boson. (A tiny bit deeper dive into the way conservation of momentum is used to find neutrinos is good for the soul. So imagine this thought experiment. Two couples are ice skating. Rather than standard skates, they wear roller skates on the ice, but with only a single ball bearing in the center front and center rear of each skate, each ball enclosed in a frictionless cup attached to the bottom of the skates. These ball bearings are what contact the ice, so the skates can get no traction in any direction from them. (To get the skaters started, we might build a figure-skater's toe pick into the skate in front of the front-most of the two ball bearings.) If we put set our skaters on the ice and pushed, they could not turn in any way. If we separated any two of them by some distance, we could push them at one another, and they would collide if our aim was good. Now let's give each pair of skaters one more piece of equipment: a smooth steel rod, about the thinkness of rebar (say, 1/2 inch); each rod is some three feet in length, enabling one skater to place hands roughly shoulder-length apart, and the second skater her own pair of hands comfortably inside the first skater's hands. Suppose we put two pairs of skaters, thus equipped, on the ice, one at each side of (say) a hockey rink, game-ready, zambonied. Grasping the rod held vertically between them, and using their toe picks just initiallty for traction, they could induce a spin around the rod, much as pairs skaters sometimes do, with no rod. But with the rod, we might use our own rod, capped as a short "T" at one end, with the crossbar turned up into a half-circle. With such a tool, we could reach quickly between the spinning skaters (digging in our own toe picks, or from side of the ice), connect with the center of their verical rod, and push the pair into a linear trajectory, even while they spin around the center of that linear motion, across the ice. Now if we were clever enough, some large enough team of us could do the same thing on the other end of the rink, pushing a 2nd spinning couple across the ice toward the first. Now, on this simple model, you can see that we might view each couple as a particle, consisting of some number of parts (perhaps three: two skaters and one rod holding them together), but moving as a whole in a single direction. If we succeed in our (maybe cruel) attempt at directing the spinning couples directly toward one another from across the rink, we'll have a collision: otherwise, not. The one thing we know about any colliding pair is that they were moving directly along the path of the collision, or it wouldn't have happened. Now imaging pushing bundles of spinning particles down a beam line, toward the center of a detector's collision hall...the one thing we know, if there is a collision, is that the sum of the weighted movements (technically, the momentum) of all the parts is all pointed right down the teamline. There is no curving away from that line--technically, momentum in a direction transverse to the beam line--if there is to be a collision:  transverse momentum of any collision is zero. Armed with that knowlege, we can reconstruct all the detected elements ...

// all I have for you is an invitation. Even whether to receive it as an invitation is up to you, and your choice, as well as mine, must cohere if there is to be a fact to the matter about whether or not it is an invitation. But not your choice--I so choose--under any cricumstances (in anger, under hallucinogens, under conditions of evident sustained inability to persuade me that you have any idea of what I am attempting), but rather your choice when you are responding to information--stimulus, interpreted by you--about what I am attempting when I issue what I take to be this invitation. In the end, what my actions mean--even whether they are actions or have meaning--emerges as a consensus between us. We interact in a stable way--we bond over this--or we don't. If there is an enduring answer to the question as to whether some set of conditions might reliably, stably produce such bonding interaction--such agreement--is an experiment that must be conducted under fairly elaborate set of conditions, like any other: GIGO; precision in, precision out. We are free to reject such precision--to reject science--if we choose, and it has no status independent of whether we would reject it under some set of richly-informed circumstances. But it may have such status; we may find that doing science, engaging the world as measurable and predictable--is an attractive way to engage it, and that there are conditions which we prefer to interpret as productive of such preference and of the stability that emerges from activity under that scientific preference. Predicting so is my preference.

This video introduces a podcast series (a Zoom conversation, broadcast live to YouTube) focused on the creation of a new science of computational politics. That science emerges from the creation of a high-information-flow network of rich communities. In a rich community, information drawn from (optimally) a full range of experience about the world by members united in a common worldview is parallel processed in communities that become richer through growth in ordered causal contact with the world as they progress. As Alasdair MacIntyre has taught us, the incommensurable differences that emerge between such communities can be overcome through information exchange that preserves such causal contact, with the historical record of such encounters between rival traditions constituting a new source of data for a new master science. This new science fills the role of Aristotelian politics, but enriched by all that we have since learned about the sciences generally and about computational science most recently. Because such a science aims at a fully integrated theoretical and practical account of the world, it requires not only new forms of communication among disciplines, but more fundamentally new forms of social arrangements where the emerging implications of thus-far-successful world views are lived out in communities whose understanding and values these worldviews express. This discussion will take a medium-resolution pass at this whole new direction for human self-understanding and organization, including how to begin leveraging available technologies for setting up a high-information-flow network of rich communities and begin to generate data from it.

What do we mean by ‘cognition’? The short answer is we don’t know because we can’t agree, and unambiguous, biologically grounded proposals are effectively non-existent. Cognition—and where it is found in the natural world—has been an inexhaustably meaty bone of contention since (in ‘western’ culture) Aristotle (384–322 BCE), for whom animals marked a singular transition [35], and (in ‘eastern’ culture) the Rig Veda (1700–1000 BCE) and associated texts, many of which admitted cognition in plants [36]. Not so long ago, it was suggested that an adequate definition would be possible when we have sufficient data [37], but this is not how it has worked out. The data available even 20 years ago ‘almost inhibited meaning’ [38]. Today the data are oceanic and meaning seems impossible without machine learning to detect relevant patterns. Defining cognition can even seem unnecessary, leaving its articulation a matter of scientific progress [39,40]. However, we do not have that luxury in this case. We cannot claim that basal cognition is a worthy research pursuit if we fail to provide at least a provisional working definition of the critical construct.
Steps toward implementing theoretically?

Taking Shettleworth as the jumping-off point, we offer the following working definition: Cognition comprises the sensory and other information-processing mechanisms an organism has for becoming familiar with, valuing, and interacting productively with features of its environment [exploring, exploiting, evading] in order to meet existential needs, the most basic of which are survival/persistence, growth/ thriving, and reproduction. [21, p. 416] This phyletically neutral definition specifies the adaptive value of cognition for an organism and has the additional virtue of differentiating cognition from metabolic functions, such as respiration, which arguably also employ mechanisms for acquiring, processing and acting on information to meet existential goals but does not involve familiarization, valuing, exploring, exploiting and evading [21]. Information remains uncharacterized but can be explicated in the biological context, as follows: A state of affairs is information for an organism if it triggers a change in physiology or behaviour relative to that state of affairs. Whatever state of affairs induces a change in physiology or interactive potential in an organism is information for that organism. (adapted from [43, pp. 17, 21]) This definition allows for regulatory stochasticity in the absence of a detectable change in environmental conditions. A fairly straightforward entailment of this approach is that cognition is a function necessary for any autonomous biological system’s survival, wellbeing and reproduction, which is an uncomfortable proposition for many. We say that whether one wishes to concede cognition to prokaryotes (for example) remains a matter of personal choice. This is not the issue before us. The issue before us is whether proceeding as though this were the case, in a biologically realistic fashion, is productive. The answer to that question, we believe, is yes.
